grid-down-food-1: When the grid goes down, the fridge, the tap and the cooker may all fail together, and what is left is a set of habits. The five keys are clean hands and surfaces, separating raw from cooked, cooking through, safe temperatures, and safe water. I found that spoilage comes in on dust, hands and tools, and each key blocks one of those routes. Write one grid-down example for each key in your own kitchen, and mark the key that would fail first in your house. Then ask what you would do about it.

Temperature is the main lever you control without power. Different authorities give slightly different numbers, so set them side by side and note where they differ. I counted spoiled vials by place and by exposure, and I would have you write the numbers down in the same way, in Celsius and Fahrenheit, with the source beside each one. Where the sources disagree, use the stricter number for the person most at risk. A figure you cannot source is a guess.

Cleaning is the first key to fail when the tap runs dry. The hidden route is often the tool or the cloth, as it was with the mercury vat in the experiment I corrected. Plan a way to keep hands and surfaces clean with little water: a measured amount, a sanitiser, a clean cloth for each job. Keep raw and cooked food apart, with separate boards and knives. Write the routine on one card and test it for a day.

Food poisoning is more serious for some people: the very young, older people, pregnant women and those with weakened defences. Make a household risk list with names, not categories. Decide what each person must not eat when the power is out, and who prepares their food. Counting who is at risk is the same habit as counting spoiled vials: it turns a worry into a number you can act on.

If you supply food regularly to the public from home, you are a food business under food law. Registration and control of hazards are rules about the same hidden routes of contamination. Read this lesson as a list of controls you can show to an inspector: what you do, how you check it, and what you record. Where the law is specific, follow the law, and where you are unsure, ask your local authority.
grid-down-food-2: The first question in a blackout is how long the cold lasts, and the answer is a clock you start when the power goes. Write the time the power went off on the fridge door. A fridge keeps food cold for a limited time if the door stays shut, and a full freezer holds longer than a half-empty one. I observed that warm, rich and exposed food spoils first, and the clock tells you how long you have before it does. Plan how you will stretch it.

Eat in the right order: cooked and opened items first, then chilled foods, then the freezer. The order saves food and cuts risk. Where sources disagree on how long a food lasts, take the shorter time for anyone at risk. I counted the spoiled vials in different places, and the lesson is that a number beats an impression. Rank the contents of your fridge and write the eating order for the first day.

When the power returns, decide by the state of the food, not by hope. Food that is still frozen or has ice crystals may be refrozen under the rules you have learned, and food that has thawed and warmed must be judged by time and temperature. Check three authorities' rules and note the strictest. Heating helps, but it does not last for ever and it does not destroy every spore. When in doubt, the rule is to throw it out.

A short audit after an outage saves you from guessing. Check packaging, dates and temperature in turn, and make a save-or-discard decision for each item. Write the decision and the reason. Keep the audit sheet with your outage log. Repeat the audit the next time, and compare: a record of decisions is the way you improve them.

The freezer is your stock, and the Food Standards Agency's advice sets the numbers for how long it holds. A short outage is unlikely to matter, and a long one will. Treat the freezer as a store with a clock. Write the contents of your freezer, with the date and the portion, so you can decide what to cook first. For a business, label and record, so you can show what you saved and why.
grid-down-food-3: Water is the fifth key, and it often fails together with the power. I compared two groups of houses that differed only in the water they used, and the lesson is that the source matters more than the look of the water. Learn the three kinds of advisory, and the water you must never use. Check your information from the official source, not from a neighbour. Write down where your water comes from and what you would do if it were declared unsafe.

Boiling is the surest method, and it must be done properly: a full rolling boil for the time your elevation requires. Write the time for your place. Let the water cool without adding anything, and store it covered. I verified each case by evidence, and you can verify the boil by timing it. Practise once so you know how long it takes and how much fuel it uses.

If you cannot boil, you can disinfect small quantities with household bleach, tablets, filters or sunlight, each with limits. Do the sum for the bleach dose by hand, and check the label for the strength. Know what each method does not remove. A rate is only as good as the numbers behind it, and a dose is the same: read the label, measure, and write down what you did.

Safe water has to reach every job in the kitchen, not just the cup. Use it for dishes, for washing produce and for infant formula, and know the rules for babies. List the jobs that use water in your kitchen and name the safe source for each. Track the amount you use in a day, so you know how much to store. A plan that lacks a number is a hope.

A business must provide separate sinks for washing food and for cleaning equipment, and must keep all equipment in good order. When the water fails, some steps must pause. Write which steps depend on water, what you will do with them, and how you will tell customers. Keep a record of the date, the decision and the reason, as I did with the houses and the water. A pause you have written down is easier to defend than one you improvised.
grid-down-food-4: I fed twelve hundred people on a costed pot, and the lesson was that fuel was the smallest line on the bill. Without power, cooking is a set of options, each with limits: what you can cook on and where. List your options and say where each may be used safely. Foods that need no cooking cost no fuel, so note them. Count what a meal costs you in fuel and time, and see which line is largest.

The commonest deadly mistake in a blackout is cooking indoors on a stove meant for outside. Carbon monoxide has no smell and no colour. Cook outside, keep fuel-burning stoves out of enclosed spaces, and learn the signs. Write the rule on the stove. I kept the heat in with covers and a controlled burn, but I never took a fire into a closed room, and neither should you.

Heat kills most food-poisoning bacteria, but only if it reaches the middle of the food. Use a clean thermometer and check the core. Thaw safely and cook from frozen only where the guidance allows. Reheat to the stated temperature. I closed the damper and covered the boiler to hold the heat, but I would not hold food warm for hours without checking the temperature, and neither should you.

Cooked food left out is a risk even after it has been cooked well. Apply the two-hour rule, and chill or discard on schedule. If someone in the household is ill, do not let them cook for others. Write the rule where everyone can see it. I costed every line of the meal, and a leftover is a line too: if you cannot keep it safe, do not count it as food.

The standard advice is to cook to a core temperature of 70 degrees for 2 minutes, and other pairs of time and temperature are equally safe. Check with a clean probe in the centre. Test your printed reheating instructions for the customer, because the customer's oven is not yours. Record the test, with the date and the result. The costing habit applies to a business too: list every step and what it takes.
grid-down-food-5: The safest grid-down food never needed a fridge. Build a stock of shelf-stable food, rotate it by date, and know what the dates mean. I put food in sealed bottles and heated them in water, and the lesson is that the method works only if the details are right. Write your stock list with dates and plan a rotation. Eat the oldest first. Check the cans and packets before the emergency, not during it.

A freezer is a store only while it has power, so treat it as a short buffer. Use it to buy time: freeze what you will need first, in portions, and know the ratings. Keep the thermometer where you can see it. Write down what you froze and when. I left room below the rim of every bottle, and a freezer needs room for air to move. Do not overfill, and label everything.

Canning can turn a harvest into a store, but a mistake can be fatal. Low-acid foods need pressure canning, and a jar you do not know the history of must be treated with suspicion. If in doubt, boil it, then discard. I did not know about microbes, and my times are not safe times for your food. Use a tested source for your food and jar size. Follow the full process and check the seal.

Some foods look fine and are not. Learn the signs of spoilage, and the other botulism risks at home, such as oil with garlic or herbs, and baked potatoes wrapped in foil and left warm. Do not taste to test. Write a short list of the signs you will check. A jar that is bulging, leaking or spurting is a jar to discard, whatever the date says.

The Food Standards Agency's rules for freezing in a business are practical: freeze as soon as the food is prepared, divide it into smaller portions, cool cooked dishes before freezing, and label everything. Defrost in the fridge. Label allergens and keep claims to what you can support. I traced failures to method, cork or vessel, and in a business the label is where a failure shows. Write the label as if an inspector will read it.
grid-down-food-6: Some disasters add contamination on top of the power cut. Floodwater can make food unsafe, and the rule is to throw away what has touched it, with the exceptions the lesson gives for sealed commercial cans. Clean the kitchen surfaces carefully. Write the save-or-discard list. I wrote about prevention first, and the best answer to a flood is to move food up and out of its reach before it arrives.

Under stress you need rules short enough to remember. Write them in short sentences that decide most cases fast: the fridge door stays shut, cooked food goes first, hands are cleaned before food. Know your own risk level, and know the numbers you must remember. Put the page on the fridge. A rule that is on the door is a rule that gets used.

In a long outage your information comes from official voices, not guesses. Know where they speak and what each one covers. If you share food, share it with care: say what is in it, how it was kept and when it was made. Know the water that cannot be made safe, and say so. Roles matter: choose who listens for official news and who writes the log.

A plan beats a panic. Put the pieces together: the clock, the risk list, the eating order, the water plan, the cooking plan. Assign each task to a named person, with a deputy. Set a date for a drill. Run it with the power off for an hour. Hold a short debrief and change one rule. Practise before the emergency, and review after.

A frozen-meal business dispatches on a schedule, and a failure on one day affects every customer on the plan. Write what you will do if the power fails on the day before dispatch, and how you will tell customers. Keep the log. Debrief after any incident and change one rule. I wanted people to drill and to learn from the faults; a business needs both.
grid-down-food-cap: The brief is a 72-hour grid-down food-safety plan for a realistic household. Name the household, its people and its risks. The plan must contain a clock, a risk list, an eating order, a water plan and a cooking plan. Write the rules short and give each task a name. I marked one habit at a time and checked it daily, and a plan you can score is a plan you can improve.

The model answer sets out the clock with real times: power off at 17:30, the fridge mark at 21:30, the half-full freezer mark at 17:30 the next day. Follow its order: the clock, the risk list, the eating order, the water, the cooking. Compare your plan with it line by line, and note where you differ and why. A model is not an answer to copy, but a shape to check yourself against.

Score your plan against the rubric, then swap with a partner. Mark each criterion with the evidence for it. Give one thing to keep and two to change, and write them down. Run a drill and hold a debrief, as a community of volunteers would. Revise the plan and date the revision. Keep the score so that you can see the improvement.

The capstone for the business is a 72-hour continuity plan for a frozen-product home catering business. Stand it on sources, show the costs, and be honest about the gaps in your evidence. Cost each line, as I did when I fed the house of industry: ingredients, fuel and labour. Say what you do not know. A plan that is honest about its limits is one a customer can trust.
